title: The Fish Doorbell
summary: Every spring, thousands of fish migrate through Utrecht’s canals towards spawning grounds, but their route is interrupted by the historic Weerdsluis lock. In 2021, the city introduced the world’s first “Fish Doorbell”: an underwater livestream lets anyone watching online press a digital bell when fish are gathering at the closed lock. The signal goes to the lock keeper, who can then open the gates when enough fish are waiting. In its first season alone, people rang the bell more than 100,000 times; the project has since become an annual fixture attracting viewers from around the world.
thoughts: I already knew about this, and had rung the doorbell! The fish doorbell is such a catchy, silly name and even if there isn't evidence that this has improved fish ecology, what a fantastic example of the reach of these kinds of citizen science initiatives. It made me wonder if we could use this kind of idea as a locally-led trigger for anticipatory action, for example people could 'ring the doorbell' when their indigenous forecast techniques are telling them a flood is coming.
image_credit: Photograph: Japiot · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: The Fish Doorbell turns a hidden ecological process into something people can notice, understand and help with. Its charm matters: a small, playful interface makes participation feel immediate rather than abstract. It is a reminder that good design can create a relationship with a problem before it asks people to care about solving it.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
The crowd-sourced data from observers ringing the fish doorbell is a great 
example of a human system (canal & locks) taking corrective responsibility 
for interrupting natural systems (access to spawning grounds) but it also 
illustrates the utility in trusting crowd-sourced data for early warning 
systems. In Togo when the national weather service could not afford to 
maintain rainfall guage @ river level readings, over 1500 Red Cross 
volunteers were trained as observers to SMS daily readings directly into a 
data base, which in turn fed a Red Cross machine learning flood prediction 
model used by communities to prepare for high water…but the government 
agencies who trained the observers do not use the data because it is not 
validated. Here at the dawn of the big data era it’s great to see the 
Weerdsluis lock using trusted crowd-sourced data!

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
This is so sweet. I sent it to a bunch of friends and family, which made
them all happy. It is lovely to share a story about people coming together
about something so sweet. What I find most interesting about the story is
the naming of the webcam a "doorbell". I think that humanization of the
process is probably what attracted so much attention, and it reminds me how
important it is to incorporate imagination and whimsy when you want to
start a movement.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
I want to believe there is a genuine interest in coming closer to nature,
curiosity... but, I also see that this seamlessly harmless experiment
represents how over and over, we think we can control nature,  that we are
to control nature,  and that ultimately, this is just another way of
greenwashing. The empty or just unjustified management of natural resources
behind the "I am improving nature" kind of message.

title: One Million Checkboxes
summary: In June 2024, developer Nolen Royalty launched One Million Checkboxes: a webpage containing one million shared checkboxes, where every tick or untick was immediately visible to everyone else. He expected a few hundred users; instead, more than half a million people visited and collectively changed boxes more than 650 million times before the site was closed two weeks later. Players quickly moved beyond random clicking, using scripts and coordinated activity to create patterns, images and even hidden messages across the shared grid.
thoughts: I think this shows how when we create something it can take on a beautiful life of its own that we perhaps couldn't have ever predicted. And I love how a group of strangers found a way to connect with the original developer.
image_credit: Nolen Royalty (Itseieio) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: One Million Checkboxes is a reminder that participation is rarely predictable from the structure we design for it. A deliberately pointless interface became a space for play, coordination, competition and collective invention because people brought their own purposes to it. Sometimes the most interesting behaviour in a system is not what its designer intended, but what emerges once many people begin interacting through it.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
We always seem to organize ourselves, we simply can’t help it. Whether
driven by competition with others or ourselves, or a desire to share what
wecare caosble of, we naturally seek structure and a sense of belonging
within a group, leading to aligning with the collective whole, or at least
most of us do!

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
William “Smitty” Smith, late founder of the National Center for Race Amity 
(Atlanta) once remarked to me that we really do not have a science of the 
human being. The I mil checkboxes Hummingbird reminds me of something that 
emerged from handling population datasculptures for dozens of countries. 
This was Pablo Suarez’s inspiration - late great climate, math & Caring 
geek! We created 3D printed population datasculptures, as an invitation to 
interrogate country data over the last 50 years or so, that presented as 
tables on a page or spreadsheet would be too boring to whip up a frenzy of 
interest. And which the datasculptures unfailingly do. At first we started 
noticing the obvious mega trends - a world war is almost indistinguishable 
from a pandemic, dramatic differences in same age male & female numbers 
highlight gender inequities at a glance & generally point to regional 
cultural drivers, however the most subtle - and perhaps most provocative of 
further investigation - is the across the board - All countries - increase 
in lifespan combined with a contraction in birth rates. Human population 
data from the past 50 years completely debunks the 1960s/70s “Population 
Bomb” theory. The classic population pyramid profile is inexorably becoming 
a population pear. There appear to be self-limiting mechanisms operating as 
a sort of hidden hive consciousness - which we scarcely recognize, let 
alone understand. What emerged from the One Million Checkboxes also 
reflects an extraordinary but surprisingly ordinary (in that we all have it 
- whatever *it* is - to hand) self-organizing capacity for co-creative 
ideation. We may collectively, as a species, be “the problem”. Human nature 
may be far less self-sustaining and vastly more hive-sustaining than we 
have yet to imagine.
Onwards!

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
Ok why did all the users not crash the site?? But thinking bigger, how do
you predict what will go viral at any given time?

title: Ise Jingu
summary:
At Ise Jingu in Japan, the main Shinto shrine buildings are completely rebuilt every 20 years in a tradition known as Shikinen Sengu. The practice dates back more than 1,300 years and requires each generation of craftspeople to recreate the buildings, furnishings and ritual objects using traditional methods. Rather than preserving the same physical structure indefinitely, the process preserves the knowledge, skills and practices needed to rebuild it.

Kyodo News illustrated feature on the current rebuilding cycle: https://immersive.kyodonews.net/ise-jingu/index.html
thoughts: We've been thinking a lot about disaster memory recently, and I generally think of memorials to floods which are in some ways designed to make sure people don't forget. However, this is a much more active way of engaging with history, and I wonder how to apply it to disasters.
image_credit: Photograph: Zairon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Ise Jingu offers a striking alternative to the idea that resilience means making something last forever. The buildings are temporary, but the capability to recreate them is deliberately renewed across generations. It suggests that continuity can depend less on preserving an object unchanged than on repeatedly practising the knowledge, relationships and skills needed to rebuild it.

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
What parts of our lives do we struggle to rebuild when they break? What
would it look like to practice that rebuilding before things break? In a
way that is celebratory rather than scared?

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
At a time when long-term perspectives and enduring, resilient, approaches
to living, particularly regarding buildings and places, are top of mind for
me, this story leaves me feeling quite divided. And it makes me wonder how
this tradition could be about enhancing places, instead of tearing them
down, passing this tradition also far beyond their immediate physical as
well as time boundaries. But I am no one to change traditions!

title: Dear Data
summary: Dear Data was a year-long project by information designers Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec. Each week, while living on opposite sides of the Atlantic, they chose one aspect of their everyday lives to track — from clocks and purchases to smiles, indecision and physical contact — then turned the data into a hand-drawn postcard and mailed it to the other person. Across 52 weeks, the project became both a record of their lives and a friendship built through data, using visualisation not just to quantify behaviour but to notice and communicate experience.
thoughts: Such a creative experiment! On one hand, what a burden to be constantly recording data on the most seemingly mundane things. But also a reminder that in general we don't capture 'data' on some of the most beautiful things, like laughter, compliments and hugs. Then also behind this is a committed friendship and an example of how a single brief can result in two often very different outcomes. I didn't realise, but this probably inspired Hummingbird (this was a pre-website Inspiration that I decided to include)
image_credit: Photograph: Sara Di Franco · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Dear Data shows that data can be a way of paying attention, not just measuring performance. By choosing what to notice and then drawing it by hand, the project turns everyday experience into something reflective and relational. It suggests that the value of data sometimes lies less in precision than in the questions it encourages us to ask about our own lives and about one another.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
I’m quite struck by how much care for the other person and human connection
this experiment/ story shows. The data points themselves, collected day by
day, might not tell us much about someone on their own. But collecting
them, bringing them together in a drawing, and posting them! to someone
else with tireless effort, that’s care, that’s dedication! Imagine if we
all approached our lives (and datashsring) and communication with this
level of care and intention. How much better could we be at joining the
dots, seeing the bigger picture and creating meaningful impact?

title: The Thing From The Future
summary: The Thing From The Future is an imagination game created by Stuart Candy and Jeff Watson in which players combine cards describing a type of future, a domain, an object and a mood, then invent an artefact that could plausibly exist in that world. The print-and-play deck contains more than 3.7 million possible prompt combinations, deliberately forcing players away from a single expected future and towards multiple, sometimes uncomfortable or surprising possibilities. The game has subsequently been adapted for workshops, education and digital play.
thoughts: This was an older inspiration that I've recycled for the website. I've used the online version a number of times to help get people into an imaginative frame of mind within meetings. It's interesting to see the differences in the 'objects' that people imagine from the same prompts, sometimes revealing something previously unknown about their personalities!
image_credit: Stuart Candy and Jeff Watson · The Thing From The Future (Print-and-Play Edition), 2015 · CC BY-NC-SA
discovery: Most planning starts by asking what is likely to happen. The Thing From The Future asks a different question: what could exist if the surrounding world changed enough? That shift matters because imagination is not the opposite of rigour; it can be a way of exposing assumptions that ordinary planning leaves untouched. A strange imagined object can make an unfamiliar future concrete enough to discuss, challenge and design for.

title: What people actually do in an emergency
summary: In 2017, an accidental explosion and small fire on a London Underground train was captured on CCTV, allowing researchers to analyse the immediate reactions of 40 passengers. Rather than a uniform response of panic and flight, they observed remarkably varied behaviours. Some passengers ran, others walked, six initially retrieved belongings, five stopped to observe what was happening, and five waited or moved aside to let others pass. Researchers identified only two instances of antisocial behaviour, alongside numerous examples of cooperation, including passengers making space for others and a parent shielding her child. The study provides unusually detailed evidence of how people behave during a real, unexpected emergency.
thoughts: The research itself points to how initial reactions to an explosion show a high degree of variability, but over time behaviour becomes more homogenous. I think this is worth considering when thinking about early warning systems and anticipating unprecedented extremes, particularly for rapid onset hazards. How do people respond to an early warning, and how do interactions with others shape that response? And if we can understand that better, how might we design early warning systems differently to account for that?
image_credit: Photograph: Dr Neil Clifton · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Disaster systems can be remarkably paternalistic, often assuming that people will panic, misunderstand uncertainty or need tightly controlled instructions. Yet real emergencies frequently show something more complex: people retain judgement, relationships and a capacity to help one another. Perhaps warning systems should leave more room for people themselves to cope intelligently when the prescribed response does not quite fit. A system designed around compliance may look very different from one designed around enabling judgement.

title: The Evolution of Trust
summary:
The Evolution of Trust is an interactive browser game by Nicky Case that uses repeated game-theory scenarios to explore how cooperation, mistrust, retaliation and forgiveness emerge between individuals. Players test different strategies against one another and can alter conditions such as the frequency of mistakes or the likelihood of meeting again, showing how small changes in the rules of interaction can produce very different collective outcomes.

Background on the game and its game-theory foundations: https://exploring-economics.org/en/discover/the-evolution-of-trust/
thoughts: Pablo Suarez used to say that “change happens at the speed of trust”. I like that this is an interactive game which speaks to that, using game theory (the prisoner's dilemma) to support a message of "Build relationships. Find win-wins. Communicate clearly"
discovery: The game shows that trust is not simply a virtue; it can be a practical condition for successful cooperation. In repeated versions of the Prisoner’s Dilemma, the best collective outcomes emerge when people expect to interact again, can communicate, find mutually beneficial arrangements, and have enough forgiveness to recover from occasional mistakes. “Build relationships. Find win-wins. Communicate clearly” is therefore not just good interpersonal advice: game theory helps explain why these behaviours can make cooperation more resilient.

title: The Wind Phone
summary: In a garden in Japan, an unconnected telephone allows people to speak to loved ones they have lost. What began as one person's response to grief has become a place of comfort for thousands of visitors.
thoughts: After the Nepal floods I started to reflect more on how a fatality shouldn't be just a statistic. This is a powerful reminder that for every death there are many people grieving that death, and that grief is carried through time. Creating gentle ways for people to grieve should be an important part of disaster response, and not just in the immediate aftermath.
image_credit: Photograph: Matthew Komatsu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: The Wind Phone demonstrates how a simple idea can transform how we understand loss. It reminds us that the consequences of a death extend far beyond the individual.
